title: Service-sector growth is not uniformly household-facing: information demand is split between business and consumer channels
source_unit: Census Bureau Quarterly Services Survey employer-firm revenue by class of customer, seasonally adjusted and not price-adjusted

denominator.unit: employer-firm revenue universe; exact establishment denominator is not disclosed in the release table

household_revenue_share.unit: percent of information-sector revenue, calculated from published customer-class levels

total_revenue_yoy_change.unit: percent, second quarter 2026 from second quarter 2025

household_revenue_yoy_change.unit: percent, second quarter 2026 from second quarter 2025

business_revenue_yoy_change.unit: percent, second quarter 2026 from second quarter 2025

observations.method: Transcribed Table 7 of the Census Quarterly Services Survey all-tables workbook. Household share is calculated as household consumers and individual users revenue divided by total information-sector revenue. Estimates are seasonally adjusted but not adjusted for price changes.
observations.uncertainty: Customer classes are firm-reported revenue classifications, not unique households, transactions, users, workers, or cultural participants. The table is an employer-firm frame and does not include the Census nonemployer operator layer. Revenue growth is nominal and cannot establish real demand, welfare, affordability, or service quality.
observations.subgroup: Information-sector employer firms; aggregate information sector only.
observations.counterinterpretation: The slower household channel may reflect price changes, classification, business-to-consumer intermediaries, durable demand saturation, or household substitution rather than weak cultural demand. Business growth may ultimately support consumer services indirectly.

observations.period: Second quarter 2026; telecommunications (NAICS 517, 5171, 5172, and other telecommunications rows as published)

denominator.unit: telecommunications employer-firm revenue universe; exact establishment denominator is not disclosed in the release table

household_revenue_share.unit: percent of telecommunications revenue, calculated from published customer-class levels

total_revenue_yoy_change.unit: percent, second quarter 2026 from second quarter 2025

household_revenue_yoy_change.unit: percent, second quarter 2026 from second quarter 2025

observations.method: Transcribed the telecommunications aggregate row in Table 7 of the Census Quarterly Services Survey all-tables workbook. Household share is calculated from the published household, business, and total revenue levels.
observations.uncertainty: The aggregate contains distinct wired, wireless, and other telecommunications businesses; the table does not reveal household-level prices, subscriptions, usage, churn, outages, access quality, or affordability. Revenue is nominal and establishment-based.
observations.subgroup: Telecommunications employer firms within the information sector.
observations.counterinterpretation: A high household revenue share does not prove broad access or consumer benefit; flat revenue can coexist with price increases, reduced usage, churn, or unequal service quality.

observations.period: Second quarter 2026; publishing industries (except Internet; NAICS 511)

denominator.unit: publishing employer-firm revenue universe; exact establishment denominator is not disclosed in the release table

household_revenue_share.unit: percent of publishing revenue, calculated from published customer-class levels

total_revenue_yoy_change.unit: percent, second quarter 2026 from second quarter 2025

household_revenue_yoy_change.unit: percent, second quarter 2026 from second quarter 2025

observations.method: Transcribed the publishing aggregate row in Table 7 of the Census Quarterly Services Survey all-tables workbook and calculated the household revenue share from published levels.
observations.uncertainty: Publishing customer classes do not identify readers, subscribers, cultural participation, attention, advertising exposure, creator income, or household media budgets. Revenue is nominal and may include intermediate business sales.
observations.subgroup: Publishing employer firms except Internet publishing; aggregate row only.
observations.counterinterpretation: Fast nominal revenue growth with a minority household share could reflect business distribution, advertising, licensing, consolidation, or price changes rather than expanding household cultural consumption.

related_sources.claim: Official second-quarter 2026 Quarterly Services Survey release: selected-services revenue was $6,418.7 billion, up 7.6% year over year and 3.0% quarter over quarter.
Official historical-data page identifies the second-quarter 2026 all-tables workbook and Quarterly Services Survey data context.
Census describes QSS as a timely source of service-industry revenue and expense indicators and notes the employer-firm and customer-class scope.

boundary: This record measures nominal employer-firm service revenue by customer class; it does not measure unique consumers, household spending, affordability, service completion, worker conditions, nonemployer receipts, attention, cultural meaning, or causal demand. It is a bridge between the nonemployer operator layer and payroll/service-firm revenue, not a pooled market-size estimate. Customer-class values marked S in the workbook are suppressed and are not imputed.
